items.readable_text:
Content:
In mathematics, there are two main types of "machines" known as automata. These structures represent the first step toward formally defining the concept of an algorithm.

Content:
The first type of automaton is called an acceptor. It processes a string of symbols and determines whether to accept or reject it. The second is called a transducer, which takes an input string and transforms it into another string. In this lesson, we will focus on acceptors.

Content:
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a specific type of acceptor. It has a finite number of states and processes symbols from an input alphabet, transitioning between states based on predefined rules determined by the input symbols.

Content:
More formally, a DFA is a five-tuple of the form [MATH: A=(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F),] where the components are as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states. These are all the possible configurations the automaton can be in.
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols. This is the "alphabet" of symbols that the DFA can process as inputs.
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state. This function determines how the DFA moves from one state to another based on a given input symbol.
- [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state). This is the state in which the automaton begins.
- [MATH: F \subseteq Q] is a set of final (or accepting) states.

Content:
We can visualize a DFA as a directed graph, where

Content:
- vertices represent the states,
- arcs, labeled with input symbols, represent transitions from one state to another,
- the start state is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to,] and
- the final states are circled by a double line.

Content:
For example, a deterministic finite automaton is given in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4be8735f80a2e8fbbb936bfc53f694b5]

Content:
In this case, the automaton has the following components:

Content:
- The set of states [MATH: Q = \{p,q\}] (represented by the vertices).
- The set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma = \{0,1,2\}] (represented by the arcs' labels).
- The transition function [MATH: \delta] with the following transitions defined by the arcs:
[MATH: δ(p, 0)|= p,|δ(p, 1)|= q,|δ(p, 2)|= p,; δ(q, 0)|= p,|δ(q, 1)|= q,|δ(q, 2)|= p]
For instance, the arrow from [MATH: p] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1,] means that [MATH: \delta(p,1)=q.]

[IMG: /graphics/546fa0d4d35d84781c40c5a0067b9104]
- The start state [MATH: p] (that is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to]), as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/4c261d07f2ccb02e41a6b341e01c4b32]
- The set of final states [MATH: F = \{q\}] (circled by the double line), as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/887645effee2202cba6e2ccb8a07f660]

A deterministic finite automaton is a five-tuple of the form [MATH: A = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F),] where

  • [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta: Q \times \Sigma \to Q] that takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state,

  • [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state), and

  • [MATH: F \subseteq Q] is a set of final (or accepting) states.

  • the set of states [MATH: Q=\{p,q,r\}] (represented by the vertices),

  • the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma=\{0,1\}] (represented by the arcs' labels),

  • the start state [MATH: q] (that is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to]), and

  • the set of final states [MATH: F=\{q,r\}] (these are circled by the double line).

Finally, the diagram shows an arrow from [MATH: q] to [MATH: r,] labeled [MATH: 1.] This means that [MATH: \delta(q,1) = r.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In our case, the automaton has the following components:

  • the set of states [MATH: Q=\{p,q,r\},]

  • the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma=\{0,1\},]

  • the start state [MATH: p,] and

  • the set of final states [MATH: F=\{q\}.]

With that in mind, let's determine the transition function.

First, we draw an empty table with a different state written in each row and a different input symbol written in each column:

[MATH: \Large _{Q} \!\backslash\! ^{\Sigma}]

[MATH: 0]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: \to \! p]

[MATH: \ast \: q]

[MATH: r]

Notice that we write [MATH: \to] next to [MATH: p] since it's the start state, and we write [MATH: \ast] next to [MATH: q] since it's a final state.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In mathematics, there are two main types of "machines" known as automata. These structures represent the first step toward formally defining the concept of an algorithm.

Content:
The first type of automaton is called an acceptor. It processes a string of symbols and determines whether to accept or reject it. The second is called a transducer, which takes an input string and transforms it into another string. In this lesson, we will focus on acceptors.

Content:
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a specific type of acceptor. It has a finite number of states and processes symbols from an input alphabet, transitioning between states based on predefined rules determined by the input symbols.

Content:
More formally, a DFA is a five-tuple of the form [MATH: A=(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F),] where the components are as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states. These are all the possible configurations the automaton can be in.
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols. This is the "alphabet" of symbols that the DFA can process as inputs.
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state. This function determines how the DFA moves from one state to another based on a given input symbol.
- [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state). This is the state in which the automaton begins.
- [MATH: F \subseteq Q] is a set of final (or accepting) states.

Content:
We can visualize a DFA as a directed graph, where

Content:
- vertices represent the states,
- arcs, labeled with input symbols, represent transitions from one state to another,
- the start state is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to,] and
- the final states are circled by a double line.

Content:
For example, a deterministic finite automaton is given in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4be8735f80a2e8fbbb936bfc53f694b5]

Content:
In this case, the automaton has the following components:

Content:
- The set of states [MATH: Q = \{p,q\}] (represented by the vertices).
- The set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma = \{0,1,2\}] (represented by the arcs' labels).
- The transition function [MATH: \delta] with the following transitions defined by the arcs:
[MATH: δ(p, 0)|= p,|δ(p, 1)|= q,|δ(p, 2)|= p,; δ(q, 0)|= p,|δ(q, 1)|= q,|δ(q, 2)|= p]
For instance, the arrow from [MATH: p] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1,] means that [MATH: \delta(p,1)=q.]

[IMG: /graphics/546fa0d4d35d84781c40c5a0067b9104]
- The start state [MATH: p] (that is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to]), as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/4c261d07f2ccb02e41a6b341e01c4b32]
- The set of final states [MATH: F = \{q\}] (circled by the double line), as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/887645effee2202cba6e2ccb8a07f660]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Components of a DFA

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/562972fb11054f334ec6f2aa869896f4]

Consider the deterministic finite automaton represented by the above diagram. Given that [MATH: \delta: Q \times \Sigma \to Q] is the transition function of the automaton, determine the set of states, the set of input symbols, the start point, and the set of final states of the automaton. Also, determine [MATH: \delta(q,1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A deterministic finite automaton is a five-tuple of the form [MATH: A = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F),] where

- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states,
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols,
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta: Q \times \Sigma \to Q] that takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state,
- [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state), and
- [MATH: F \subseteq Q] is a set of final (or accepting) states.

In our case, the automaton has the following components:

- the set of states [MATH: Q=\{p,q,r\}] (represented by the vertices),
- the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma=\{0,1\}] (represented by the arcs' labels),
- the start state [MATH: q] (that is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to]), and
- the set of final states [MATH: F=\{q,r\}] (these are circled by the double line).

Finally, the diagram shows an arrow from [MATH: q] to [MATH: r,] labeled [MATH: 1.] This means that
[MATH: \delta(q,1) = r.]

---

[IMG: /graphics/q-257520]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Transition Tables of Deterministic Finite Automata

Content:
It's common to put the values of a transition function in a table. Each row corresponds to a different state [MATH: q,] each column corresponds to a different input symbol [MATH: a,] and their intersection is the value of the transition function [MATH: \delta(q,a).]

Content:
An example is given below.
Note that we place [MATH: \to] next to the start state and [MATH: \ast] next to any final states.

Content:
| [MATH: \Large _{Q} \!\backslash\! ^{\Sigma}] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \to \! p] | [MATH: p] | [MATH: q] |
| [MATH: \ast \: q] | [MATH: q] | [MATH: q] |

Content:
Let's construct a diagram representing the automaton given by this transition table.
From the table, we determine that the automaton has the following components:

Content:
- the set of states [MATH: Q=\{p,q\}] (given by the rows),
- the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma=\{0,1\}] (given by the columns),
- the start state [MATH: p] (labeled by [MATH: \to]), and
- the set of final states [MATH: F=\{q\}] (labeled by [MATH: \ast]).

Content:
Now that we have the components, we can construct the diagram.
First, let's draw the states of our automaton.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33f10abe5ff2d9c249de0f394010a2e3]

Content:
According to the transition table, [MATH: p] is the start state, and [MATH: q] is a final state. So, we labeled [MATH: p] with an input arrow and circled [MATH: q] with a double line.

Content:
From the transition table, we also get the following:

Content:
- Consider row [MATH: p] of the table.

- Its intersection with column [MATH: 0] is [MATH: p,] indicating that [MATH: \delta(p,0)=p.] So, we draw an arrow (loop) from [MATH: p] to [MATH: p,] labeled [MATH: 0.]
- Its intersection with column [MATH: 1] is [MATH: q,] indicating that [MATH: \delta(p,1)=q.] So, we draw an arrow from [MATH: p] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/403a3c4335095a1062ba7b3517f77a52]

Content:
- Consider row [MATH: q] of the table.

- Its intersection with column [MATH: 0] is [MATH: q,] indicating that [MATH: \delta(q,0)=q.] So, we draw an arrow (loop) from [MATH: q] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 0.]
- Its intersection with column [MATH: 1] is [MATH: q,] indicating that [MATH: \delta(q,1)=q.] So, we draw an arrow (loop) from [MATH: q] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1.]

In our case, the automaton has the following components:

- the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma=\{0,1\},]
- the start state [MATH: p,] and
- the set of final states [MATH: F=\{q\}.]

With that in mind, let's determine the transition function.

First, we draw an empty table with a different state written in each row and a different input symbol written in each column:

| [MATH: \Large _{Q} \!\backslash\! ^{\Sigma}] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \to \! p] | | |
| [MATH: \ast \: q] | | |
| [MATH: r] | | |

Notice that we write [MATH: \to] next to [MATH: p] since it's the start state, and we write [MATH: \ast] next to [MATH: q] since it's a final state.

Next, we fill in the remaining cells:

- There is an arrow (loop) from [MATH: p] to [MATH: p,] labeled [MATH: 0.] This means that [MATH: \delta(p,0)=p.] So, we write [MATH: p] at the intersection of row [MATH: p] and column [MATH: 0.]
- There is an arrow from [MATH: p] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1.] This means that [MATH: \delta(p,1)=q.] So, we write [MATH: q] at the intersection of row [MATH: p] and column [MATH: 1.]
- There is an arrow from [MATH: q] to [MATH: p,] labeled [MATH: 0.] This means that [MATH: \delta(q,0)=p.] So, we write [MATH: p] at the intersection of row [MATH: q] and column [MATH: 0.]
- There is an arrow from [MATH: q] to [MATH: r,] labeled [MATH: 1.] This means that [MATH: \delta(q,1)=r.] So, we write [MATH: r] at the intersection of row [MATH: q] and column [MATH: 1.]
- There is an arrow from [MATH: r] to [MATH: p,] labeled [MATH: 0.] This means that [MATH: \delta(r,0)=p.] So, we write [MATH: p] at the intersection of row [MATH: r] and column [MATH: 0.]
- There is an arrow (loop) from [MATH: r] to [MATH: r,] labeled [MATH: 1.] This means that [MATH: \delta(r,1)=r.] So, we write [MATH: r] at the intersection of row [MATH: r] and column [MATH: 1.]

The transition table corresponding to the given diagram is shown below.

| [MATH: \Large _{Q} \!\backslash\! ^{\Sigma}] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \to \! p] | [MATH: p] | [MATH: q] |
| [MATH: \ast \: q] | [MATH: p] | [MATH: r] |
| [MATH: r] | [MATH: p] | [MATH: r] |
